It's a koosh - it isn't going to hurt anything. Of COURSE drones aren't cheap - which is why you shouldn't fly them around in public places where people play ball, frisbee, koosh, etc - it's like those guys that wanted to fly their drones over the ocean, then whined and cried when they crashed them into the water. Why? Why would you be upset about that? You had to know there was a chance that would happen when you thought that was a good idea.

You're right - it's a public park. For everyone. Meaning OP has no right to ask the drone operator to do anything, and the drone operator has no right to ask people to be mindful of his stuff. It's in the public. Let's look at this a different way

Let's say instead of a drone it was a dog with a camera on it. ('But a drone isn't a dog!' I hear you whine 'It isn't controllable like a drone is!' A drone on a windy day is uncontrollable - it could crash and slice the jugular of a little kiddie on its way down. Once a drone reaches a certain size/weight, the lift needed to get it up means those blades could take off fingers. Monkeys could fly out of our butts. Life is chaos. Follow me here.) The dog is unknown to children in the park and is getting a little too close for parental comfort. Maybe it's barking and following the kids around (at a distance, but the parents are unfamiliar with it and don't know how trained the dog is - just like they don't know how trained the drone operator is. See? See where I'm going with this?). Let's say it's a purebred husky, or Sheppard - some breed of dog that costs a lot to have a pure-bred form of and people would recognize that purely from looking at it. Does that mean the people in the park owe the dog owner something because the dog looks expensive? No, of course not - that's silly. If the drone operator cared about his/her drone s/he would be nearby. People could approach him/her like adults, s/he could respond like an adult, and everyone could get on with their lives.

In a public setting if something within reason is upsetting all the kids at a public park, you should probably move on. If it's one whiny parent, that's something completely different. BUT I always like to err on the side of caution when it comes to kids; I don't think some of the bigger drones should be in public parks near unpredictable children. The fact of the matter is kids will walk into a goddamn woodchipper if given the chance. They aren't smart. Because they're kids. They wouldn't know to stay away from the blade of a drone landing because the wind picked up - they'd walk over and shove their cherubic little faces/fingers right into the blades because it's a shiny toy plane. Because kids are dumb like that.

This whole idea that 'I spent a lot of money on it so people shouldn't touch it' is dumb. If you spent so much money on it, treat it like you spent a lot of money on it - take care of it. That means acknowledging that while it is in a public place it could be subject to damages that it would not normally be exposed to if it was in a private residence. That's the public part of public park. I have a couple little quad copters I take to my local park. (I know, they aren't drones - but they are mine, weren't all cheap, and I like them.) I keep the more expensive ones at home because the park has a tennis court. Has a ball ever made it up to my li'l copter? Nope. But I acknowledge there's a chance, so the copters I have the most parts for go with me, not the pricier ones. Because an adult that spends money on something expensive should know to take care of it.
